THE LEGAL GAP Laws that come close, but don't cover it 1 BNSS ss. 105–106: search, seizure and video recording. Nothing on unlocking or copying a phone. 2 IT Act s. 69: decryption needs a written Home Secretary order. Challenged in the Supreme Court since 2019; pending. 3 BSA s. 63: certifies electronic records for court; it doesn't make the extraction lawful. 4 DPDP Act s. 17: exempts processing for investigation (in force from May 2027). PRACTICAL CHECKLIST If your phone is seized 1 Get the seizure memo listing the device, and note that the search must be video-recorded (BNSS s. 105). 2 Ask that the hash value be recorded at seizure, so later tampering can be detected. 3 Take legal advice before giving passwords. The law on compelled passwords is unsettled. 4 Lawyers and journalists: flag privileged and source material in writing (BSA s. 132 for lawyers). 5 Apply for return of the device (BNSS s. 497), and for deletion of copied data if you're not charged. TA K E AWAY A phone holds a whole life. The law should say who can open it. India is buying phone-cracking tools faster than it is writing rules for them. Until Parliament or the Supreme Court fills the gap, know your rights at the moment of seizure. Adv.
